title: Ski & Snowboard Resorts in the US
one_liner: US ski resorts are a mature, weather-exposed leisure industry where multi-resort passes, destination spending and summer activities are cushioning volatile snowfall.
overview: The industry operates downhill, cross-country and related ski areas, including lifts, snowmaking, ski schools, rentals, food and beverage and four-season mountain activities, while excluding separately owned lodging-only assets. Demand is discretionary and seasonal, but the post-pandemic period has shown unusually durable visitation: US ski areas recorded 61.5 million skier visits in the 2024-25 season, up 1.7% from 2023-24 and the second-highest season on record. The main strategic shift since the 2022 baseline is that revenue is less dependent on walk-up lift tickets and more dependent on advance-commitment products such as Epic Pass and Ikon Pass, which stabilize cash flow but concentrate industry power among large operators. Weather volatility remains the central risk: even with strong 2024-25 national visits, below-average snowfall and a historically difficult 2025-26 western season hurt destination visitation and ancillary spending at major resorts.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $5.4 billion in US ski resort industry sales; an alternate January 2026 Kentley listing estimated 2025 revenue at $5.0 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025: 10.9% average annual sales growth in the July 2026 Kentley/ResearchAndMarkets listing; the January 2026 Kentley listing reported 7.8% average annual growth over the prior five years.
key_stats.skier_visits: 2024-25: 61.5 million US skier visits, up 1.7% from 2023-24 and second-highest on record.
key_stats.operating_areas: 2024-25: 492 US ski areas in operation, up from 484 in 2023-24.
key_stats.capital_spending: 2024-25: US resorts invested $624.4 million in improvements; 2025-26 planned capital spending was $560.7 million, including 47 new lifts and 70 lift upgrades.
key_stats.pass_mix: 2024-25: season passes accounted for 49% of US skier visits, while lift tickets accounted for 32%.
key_stats.snowfall: 2024-25: average US resort snowfall was 150 inches, about 7% below 2023-24 and below the 10-year average of 175 inches.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2021: $2.541 billion in industry revenue in the IBISWorld baseline file, presented in 2021 dollars.
baseline_2022.growth: 2016-2021: revenue declined at a 2.9% annualized rate; 2021 revenue fell 6.2%.
baseline_2022.profit: 2021: $175 million profit, equal to a 6.9% profit margin.
baseline_2022.forecast_at_baseline: 2021-2026: IBISWorld baseline projected revenue growth of 6.7% annually to $3.5 billion in 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Resorts earn revenue from lift tickets and season passes, ski and snowboard lessons, equipment rental and retail, food and beverage, event services, summer sightseeing and mountain biking, parking and guest services. Large destination operators also benefit indirectly from adjacent lodging, real estate, transportation and village spending, even when those lines are reported outside the core ski-area industry.
cost_structure: The largest costs are seasonal labor for lift operations, patrol, instructors, food service and maintenance; energy, water and maintenance for snowmaking; lift and mountain infrastructure depreciation; insurance and safety compliance; resort fees and land-use permits; food, beverage and retail cost of goods; marketing, technology and pass-platform costs; and capital spending on lifts, snowmaking, terrain, employee housing and summer activities. In 2025, Vail Resorts' mountain segment reported $760.955 million of labor and labor-related benefits and $1.812 billion of total mountain operating expense against $2.630 billion of mountain net revenue.
major_players: Vail Resorts: in fiscal 2025, operated 42 destination mountain resorts and regional ski areas globally, generated $2.630 billion of mountain net revenue and reported 17.665 million skier visits.
Alterra Mountain Company: in 2026, listed 19 owned North American destinations and used Ikon Pass to connect owned and partner mountains across 13 countries and 5 continents.
Boyne Resorts: in 2026, described itself as the largest independent mountain resort company in North America and remains privately held by the Kircher family.

POWDR and related independent owners: POWDR sold Killington and Pico in 2024 and said it would rebalance toward Copper Mountain, Snowbird, Woodward and national-park concessions, illustrating ongoing portfolio churn.

Independent and regional ski areas: small and midsize operators remain important for local day-ski demand, beginner conversion and Midwest/East Coast resilience, but face higher relative capital and weather risk.
current_dynamics: The 2025-26 operating environment is mixed. The 2024-25 season proved demand durability with 61.5 million visits despite below-average snowfall, but 2025-26 western weather exposed how quickly destination traffic, ski school, dining and rentals can weaken. Vail Resorts reported North American season-to-date skier visits down 14.9% through April 19, 2026, and then cut fiscal 2026 Resort EBITDA guidance to $735 million-$755 million in June 2026. Advance pass revenue is cushioning operators, but softer 2026-27 pass sales show that poor prior-season conditions can delay or reduce renewals. Capital spending remains heavy as resorts upgrade lifts, snowmaking and summer attractions to protect guest experience and broaden revenue beyond winter.
whats_growing: Advance-commitment season passes, frequency products, premium destination pricing, summer sightseeing and bike-park activity, snowmaking investment, lift upgrades, app-based guest engagement, younger-adult pass offers and small-to-midsize ski area visitation all gained strategic importance in 2024-2026. The 2024-25 Pacific Northwest region set a record with 4.7 million visits, while the Midwest rebounded 21.8% after a weak 2023-24 season.
whats_shrinking: Weather-sensitive destination visits, walk-up lift-ticket reliance, lower-capital independent ownership, weak-snow western traffic and some legacy retail/rental spend are under pressure. Vail Resorts reported 2026 North American skier visits down 14.9% through April 19, 2026, ski school revenue down 12.0% and dining revenue down 11.7%, highlighting shrinkage in ancillary spending when visits fall.
recent_developments: 2024-09: Killington and Pico completed a sale from POWDR to local investors, with $30 million pledged for upgrades including snow guns, a six-pack lift and gondola cabins.
2025-05: NSAA preliminary data showed 61.5 million US skier visits in 2024-25, up 1.7% from 2023-24 and second-highest on record.
2025-05: US resorts reported $624.4 million of 2024-25 capital improvements and planned $560.7 million for 2025-26, including 47 new lifts and 70 lift upgrades.
2025-09: Ikon Pass expanded its 2025-26 network with additional destinations including Ischgl in Austria and other European access, reinforcing pass competition.
2026-04: Vail Resorts said North American season-to-date skier visits were down 14.9% through April 19, 2026 after unfavorable western weather.
2026-06: Vail Resorts reduced fiscal 2026 Resort EBITDA guidance to $735 million-$755 million and reported early 2026-27 pass unit sales down about 10% through May 26, 2026.
outlook: Through 2026, the industry remains larger than the 2022 baseline but more dependent on pricing power, pass renewals and capital intensity than on pure participation growth. A normal-snow 2026-27 season would likely restore some visitation, because multi-resort passholders remain committed and the national four-year run above 60 million skier visits suggests a higher demand baseline than before 2020. The downside case is not a collapse in interest but margin compression: weak snow raises snowmaking and labor inefficiency, lowers destination ancillary spend and forces more discounting for late-cycle pass sales. Larger operators are positioned to keep consolidating share through lift upgrades, snowmaking, data-driven pass pricing and year-round revenue, while smaller resorts need local loyalty, beginner conversion and disciplined capex to remain competitive.

title: Sleep Disorder Clinics
one_liner: Outpatient sleep clinics diagnose and manage sleep apnea, insomnia, narcolepsy and related disorders through consultations, sleep testing and therapy support.
overview: The industry consists of outpatient clinics, often independent, physician-owned, hospital-owned or affiliated with academic medical centers, that evaluate and treat sleep disorders. Revenue is anchored by physician consultations, polysomnography and home sleep apnea testing, CPAP setup and follow-up, and a smaller amount of research or grant-funded work. The market is fragmented, with low concentration, because many facilities are local specialist practices or hospital departments rather than national chains. Current growth is being pulled by obesity-linked obstructive sleep apnea, aging demographics, better awareness of the cardiovascular and metabolic risks of untreated sleep disorders, and telemedicine-enabled pathways. The main structural shift is from expensive in-lab sleep studies toward home sleep apnea testing for uncomplicated adults, with complex cases, negative home tests and non-OSA disorders still supporting lab-based demand.

key_stats.market_size: $13.6 billion in 2026, estimated by applying the published 8.2% 2021-2028 CAGR to a $9.20 billion 2021 U.S. sleep disorder clinics market base
key_stats.growth: 8.2% CAGR from 2021 to 2028, with 2026 implied year-over-year growth of 8.2%
key_stats.sleep_disorder_population: 50 million to 70 million Americans with sleep disorders, cited by NHLBI in 2025
key_stats.osa_population: 83.7 million U.S. adults estimated to have obstructive sleep apnea in 2024
key_stats.short_sleep_prevalence: 30.5% of U.S. adults had short sleep duration in 2024

baseline_2022.market_size: $9.7 billion in 2022, estimated from the baseline IBISWorld 2021 revenue of $9.344 billion and its 3.5% 2021-2026 forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: 3.5% implied 2022 growth under the baseline IBISWorld 2021-2026 outlook
baseline_2022.baseline_context: The baseline file reported 2021 revenue of $9.344 billion, 2021 profit margin of 12.7%, 3,318 establishments and a 2026 revenue forecast of $11.1 billion.

how_it_makes_money: Clinics bill private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid and self-pay patients for initial and follow-up sleep-medicine consultations, diagnostic in-lab polysomnography, home sleep apnea testing, CPAP titration and therapy-management visits. Some operators also earn revenue from CPAP masks, hoses, filters and other supplies, while hospital and academic centers may receive grant or sponsored-study revenue for sleep research.
cost_structure: The model is labor-heavy, led by physician, respiratory therapist, sleep technologist, nursing, scheduling and billing wages. Other major costs include rent or hospital overhead for sleep labs, diagnostic equipment, monitoring software, CPAP and mask inventory where sold, medical supplies, malpractice and accreditation compliance, payer documentation, billing and collections. Profitability depends on utilization of staffed sleep rooms, payer mix, reimbursement rates, denial rates and the share of lower-cost home tests versus higher-revenue lab studies.
major_players: Academic medical centers such as Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic and UCLA
ResMed/VirtuOx as an adjacent home-diagnostics platform rather than a traditional clinic chain
current_dynamics: Demand is strong but the delivery model is changing. Payers and Medicare contractors continue to support home sleep apnea testing for appropriate uncomplicated OSA patients, which expands access but reduces reliance on higher-priced lab studies. AASM guidance keeps physician oversight central, limiting a full shift to automated consumer screening. The FDA's 2024 approval of tirzepatide for some obese adults with moderate-to-severe OSA creates a new adjunct or alternative pathway, while implantable nerve-stimulation devices and connected CPAP platforms broaden referral and follow-up activity. Philips Respironics' 2024 consent decree and 2025 DreamStation recall issues continued to affect CPAP supply, patient confidence and therapy management workflows.
whats_growing: Home sleep apnea testing, telehealth consultations, post-discharge OSA evaluation, CPAP adherence monitoring, connected-device data review, treatment of obesity-linked OSA, and public-insurance-covered sleep care are growing. CPAP therapy remains an important revenue line, while drug therapy and implantable stimulation are creating more multidisciplinary referral pathways.
whats_shrinking: Routine in-lab testing for uncomplicated suspected OSA is losing share to home testing. Standalone labs dependent on high volumes of polysomnography face margin pressure from reimbursement limits, payer prior authorization, documentation requirements and competition from primary care, telehealth, DME-linked diagnostics and sleep-aid substitutes.
recent_developments: 2024-04: FDA announced a federal consent decree restricting Philips Respironics' U.S. production and sale of many new CPAP, BiPAP and related respiratory devices until compliance requirements are met.
2024-06: AASM reported more than 2,300 accredited sleep centers across the United States.
2024-12: FDA approved Zepbound (tirzepatide) as the first drug treatment for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.
2025-05: AASM reaffirmed that home sleep apnea testing is appropriate for uncomplicated adults at increased risk of moderate-to-severe OSA but must be ordered and interpreted under medical oversight.
2025-08: FDA approved Nyxoah's Genio System 2.1 implantable OSA therapy for eligible adults who fail or cannot tolerate standard treatments.
2026-04: CDC/NCHS reported that in 2024, 30.5% of adults had short sleep duration, 15.4% had trouble falling asleep and 18.1% had trouble staying asleep.
outlook: The industry should keep expanding through 2028 as untreated OSA and chronic sleep difficulties remain widespread and as health systems increasingly treat sleep as part of cardiometabolic care. The strongest operators will combine sleep-medicine clinicians, home testing, payer documentation discipline, CPAP adherence support and referrals for drug, dental, ENT or implantable-device options. Growth is likely to be faster in patient volume than in lab-study revenue because reimbursement and payer protocols favor cheaper diagnostic pathways. Fragmentation should persist, but platform acquisitions and hospital network integration may make back-office scale, digital monitoring and referral capture more important competitive advantages.

title: Small Specialty Retail Stores in the US
one_liner: A fragmented Main Street retail category where niche product expertise and local convenience compete against online marketplaces, big-box pricing and rising compliance costs.
overview: The industry remains mature, highly fragmented and locally oriented, with no major player approaching a dominant share. IBISWorld estimated 2025 revenue at $68.4 billion, up 2.0% in 2025 and at a 4.0% CAGR over 2020-2025, compared with the 2022 baseline of $44.6 billion in 2022 dollars. Growth is being supported by resilient consumer spending, specialty demand in higher-income trade areas and e-commerce adoption by independent retailers, while margins are pressured by big-box competition, online price transparency, wage costs, rent and tariff-driven landed-cost volatility. Tobacco products and smokers' accessories remain the largest product family, but cigarette volume pressure and FDA scrutiny are pushing operators toward vape, nicotine pouch, premium cigar, accessories, home goods and collectible niches.

key_stats.ecommerce_share_of_total_retail: 16.8% of US retail sales in Q1 2026, not seasonally adjusted
key_stats.broader_retail_growth: NRF forecast 2025 US retail sales growth of 2.7%-3.7% to $5.42-$5.48 trillion and 2026 growth of 4.4%

baseline_2022.product_mix: Tobacco products and smokers' accessories 36.8%, home goods 31.2%, collectibles and monuments 15.3%, other 12.6%, groceries and alcoholic beverages 4.1% in 2022

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn retail markups on specialized merchandise bought from wholesalers, manufacturers, importers and distributors. Revenue is largely transaction-based, with higher margins coming from curated assortments, premium tobacco and accessories, pool and home goods expertise, collectibles, monuments, custom orders, local convenience, repairs or add-on services, and in-store customer advice that mass merchants and marketplaces cannot easily replicate.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost item; wholesale merchandise costs dominate revenue, especially tobacco, imported gifts, home goods, pool supplies and collectibles.
cost_structure.wages: $5.486 billion in 2022, equal to about 12.3% of 2022 revenue; wage pressure remains a 2025-2026 margin constraint.
cost_structure.rent_and_occupancy: Meaningful fixed cost because stores need visible local locations, but many operators use small footprints to limit exposure.
cost_structure.marketing_and_payment_costs: Digital advertising, marketplace fees, card processing and loyalty tools are rising as stores add omnichannel capabilities.
cost_structure.profit_margin: 4.3% in 2022 baseline; IBISWorld described 2025 profit as under pressure from online competition and rising operating costs.

major_players: Independent tobacco, vape, cigar, pool-supply, collectible, monument, gift and home-goods retailers
Online marketplaces and big-box retailers as external competitors
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is expanding in nominal terms, but performance is uneven. Stronger consumer spending and local service-based niches are helping the top line, while shoppers remain price sensitive and increasingly use e-commerce for discovery, comparison and replenishment. The Census/FRED e-commerce share reached 16.8% of total retail sales in Q1 2026, keeping pressure on brick-and-mortar specialty stores. Tariffs and the 2025 end of de minimis treatment for many low-value imports raised landed-cost uncertainty for retailers dependent on imported niche goods. Tobacco and vape operators face a mixed environment: youth e-cigarette use declined to 1.44 million current users in 2025, but flavored disposables and nicotine pouches remain enforcement priorities and product authorization status is increasingly important at the retail shelf.
whats_growing: Omnichannel specialty retailers using local inventory, curbside pickup, social commerce and targeted e-commerce to extend reach in 2025-2026.
Premium, curated and service-heavy niches where shoppers value advice, fitting, repair, customization or local availability.
Nicotine pouches and authorized vape products, although 2025 youth use data and 2026 FDA enforcement raise compliance risk.
Home, pool, garden and hobby categories tied to household discretionary spending and project-based purchases.
Retailers in dense population centers and higher-income trade areas where traffic, events and specialty shopping trips are stronger.
whats_shrinking: Traditional cigarette-led tobacconists as adult smoking declines and regulatory scrutiny increases.
Undifferentiated gift, novelty and commodity specialty stores exposed to Amazon, Temu-style marketplaces, warehouse clubs and discount chains.
Small retailers unable to absorb 2025 tariff and de minimis cost changes without raising prices.
Stores in weak traffic corridors where rent, wages and shrink are rising faster than sales.
Operators dependent on unauthorized flavored vape or tobacco products after 2025-2026 FDA marketing and enforcement actions.
recent_developments: Jan. 23, 2025: Coresight Research projected about 15,000 US store closures in 2025 versus about 5,800 openings, signaling weaker brick-and-mortar conditions for marginal retailers.
Apr. 2, 2025: NRF forecast 2025 US retail sales growth of 2.7%-3.7% to $5.42-$5.48 trillion, with online and nonstore sales expected to grow 7%-9%.
May 2, 2025: CBP ended duty-free de minimis treatment for China-origin low-value shipments, raising landed-cost and paperwork exposure for import-reliant small retailers.
Jul. 17, 2025: FDA granted marketing orders for JUUL devices and Virginia tobacco and menthol JUULpods, clarifying part of the authorized vape shelf.
May 20, 2026: FDA warned eight retailers over unauthorized tobacco products designed to resemble candy, breath strips or cough drops.
Jul. 28, 2026: The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell to 90.8 in July 2026, pointing to softer discretionary-spending sentiment.
outlook: Revenue is likely to keep growing slowly through 2026, but gains should trail stronger retail channels unless operators offer clear product expertise, immediacy, events, service or compliant nicotine assortments. Broad retail demand is supported by NRF's 4.4% 2026 retail sales forecast, but the industry faces persistent pressure from e-commerce, tariff-related cost pass-through, high labor and occupancy costs, and tighter tobacco and vape enforcement. The better-positioned stores will be local specialists with disciplined inventory, supplier diversification, digital ordering and a premium or service-based reason for shoppers to visit.
themes: Tariff and de minimis cost pressure

title: Smart Meter Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. smart meter manufacturers are shifting from first-time AMI rollouts toward grid-edge, replacement, water-meter and software-enabled metering demand.
overview: The industry manufactures smart meters and related communications modules that record utility consumption and transmit interval data for billing, outage response, demand response, distributed-energy integration and water-loss management. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline put U.S. industry revenue at $5.791 billion, with electric meters representing 65.0% of 2021 revenue, gas meters 20.3% and water meters 14.7%. Current demand remains strongest in electric AMI, but the market is maturing: EIA reported 140.5 million U.S. electric AMI meters in 2024, equal to 83.6% of all electric meters, so growth is increasingly tied to AMI 2.0 replacements, grid-edge sensing, communications upgrades, cybersecurity, meter-data software and water AMI rather than simple penetration gains.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. smart meter market revenue estimated at $6.53 billion; 2026 revenue estimated at $7.10 billion by Grand View Research Horizon.
key_stats.growth: 2026-2033 U.S. smart meter market CAGR projected at 5.1% by Grand View Research Horizon; Mordor estimates U.S. unit volume growth at a 4.11% CAGR from 25.94 million units in 2026 to 31.73 million units in 2031.
key_stats.installed_base: 2024 U.S. electric AMI installations totaled 140,491,981, up 10.0% from 127,764,365 in 2023, according to EIA Form EIA-861.
key_stats.penetration: 2024 AMI meters were 83.6% of total U.S. electric meters; residential AMI totaled 123,019,799 meters, or 83.9% of residential electric meters.
key_stats.legacy_decline: 2024 AMR meters fell to 19,250,287 from 22,730,388 in 2023, while standard non-AMR/AMI meters fell to 8,343,731 from 15,740,422.
key_stats.federal_support: DOE Smart Grid Grants provide up to $3.0 billion over fiscal years 2022-2026, and DOE announced $3.46 billion of GRIP awards in 2023 and nearly $2.0 billion more in 2024.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 U.S. industry revenue estimated at $5.95 billion, derived from the baseline 2021 revenue of $5.791 billion and the baseline projected 2021-2027 CAGR of 2.71%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated growth: 2.71%, using the IBISWorld baseline forecast rate.
baseline_2022.installed_base: 2022 U.S. electric AMI installations totaled 118,722,741, equal to 72.3% of all electric meters, according to EIA Form EIA-861.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2021 baseline product mix: electric meters 65.0%, gas meters 20.3%, water meters 14.7%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell smart electric, gas and water meters, communications endpoints, network gear and bundled AMI systems to investor-owned utilities, municipal utilities, cooperatives and water authorities. Revenue is also earned from installation support, firmware, meter data management, network-as-a-service, analytics, maintenance and extended warranties. Large contracts are commonly multi-year deployment programs with hardware shipped over time and software or services recognized over contract life.

cost_structure.components_and_materials: Largest cost bucket in 2025-2026, including semiconductors, circuit boards, communications modules, sensors, housings, batteries and metrology components; tariff and electronics supply risk remain important pricing variables.
cost_structure.labor: Skilled manufacturing, quality, installation-support and engineering labor remain material costs; the 2021 baseline reported $1.290 billion in wages across the industry.
cost_structure.r_and_d: R&D is rising as suppliers embed edge computing, cellular, RF mesh, Wi-SUN, cybersecurity, voltage monitoring and DER visibility into meters.
cost_structure.software_and_cloud: A growing cost and margin center as manufacturers bundle meter data management, head-end systems, analytics and network operations with devices.
cost_structure.logistics_and_compliance: Costs include testing, utility certification, cybersecurity compliance, warranty reserves, project management and domestic or nearshore supply-chain adjustments.

current_dynamics: The electric-meter market is no longer an early rollout market in many states because 2024 AMI penetration reached 83.6% nationally, but utilities are still buying for replacement cycles, lagging territories, resilience investments, dynamic pricing, DER integration and outage visibility. Demand is strongest where load growth is stressing distribution networks: EIA forecast U.S. electricity demand growth in 2025 and 2026, with rapid growth in ERCOT and PJM tied to data centers, manufacturing and electrification. Federal GRIP and Smart Grid Grant funding is helping utilities justify advanced metering, sensors, communications and software. Competition is concentrated among Itron, Landis+Gyr, Sensus/Xylem, Aclara and Honeywell, while margins depend on electronics sourcing, contract timing, software attachment and tariff exposure.
whats_growing: AMI 2.0 and grid-edge meters with high-resolution sensing, voltage monitoring and edge computing.
Water AMI, leak detection and cellular communications for municipal water systems.
Software-enabled revenue from meter data management, analytics, prepay, demand response and network-as-a-service.
Deployments in regions with data-center and industrial load growth, especially Texas/ERCOT and PJM-linked markets.
Open communications standards such as Wi-SUN FAN 1.1 and cellular NB-IoT/5G options.
whats_shrinking: Legacy AMR meters, which declined from 22.7 million in 2023 to 19.3 million in 2024.
Standard non-AMR/AMI electric meters, which declined from 15.7 million in 2023 to 8.3 million in 2024.
First-wave mass deployments in saturated Western and high-penetration states, where demand is shifting toward replacement and functionality upgrades.
Standalone hardware-only sales as utilities increasingly procure integrated hardware, communications, software and services.
Low-margin commodity meters exposed to import competition and component-cost pressure.
recent_developments: 2024-10-18: DOE announced nearly $2.0 billion for 38 GRIP projects, following $3.46 billion of GRIP awards announced on 2023-10-18.

2025-01-14: Landis+Gyr announced Southwestern Electric Cooperative would deploy its Revelo grid-sensing AMI platform; the company cited more than 5 million Revelo meters under contract in North America.
2025-09-17: Itron announced American Samoa Power Authority would deploy Itron AMI smart electric meters, UtilityIQ and iPay software.
2025-12-09: Itron announced Tucson Water would deploy 250,000 smart water communication modules, with the project beginning in Q3 2025 and expected to finish by year-end 2029.
2026-01-12: DOE relaunched Digitizing Utilities Prize Round 3 with more than $2.4 million for grid-data and resilience solutions.
2026-04-08: Landis+Gyr completed the divestment of its EMEA business after reporting FY2025 continuing-operation revenue of $1.166 billion and Americas revenue of $1.040 billion.
outlook: The 2026-2031 outlook is positive but more selective than the early rollout phase. Unit shipments should keep growing as U.S. smart meter volume moves from 25.94 million units in 2026 toward 31.73 million units in 2031, while revenue growth is helped by richer functionality and software attachment. Replacement of first-generation AMI, water AMI adoption, data-center load growth, electrification and DER integration should offset slower housing-driven meter additions. Risks include utility rate-case delays, cybersecurity requirements, import tariffs, component shortages and price competition in standard meter hardware.

title: Smart Thermostat Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US smart thermostat manufacturers are shifting from early smart-home adoption toward lower-cost devices, utility demand response, and whole-home energy management.
overview: This industry designs, assembles, imports, brands, and sells smart thermostats that connect to HVAC systems and home automation platforms through Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Thread, Matter, Bluetooth, RedLINK, or related protocols. Demand comes mainly from residential replacement and remodel activity, HVAC contractors, utilities, retailers, builders, and light-commercial buildings seeking automated climate control, energy reporting, remote access, and demand response capability. The 2020 IBISWorld baseline described a young growth industry with 2020 revenue of $2.453 billion and a 2020-2025 revenue forecast of $5.5 billion, but current 2025 market estimates are more conservative, with Grand View Research estimating the US smart thermostat market at $2.68 billion in 2025 and a 2025-2030 CAGR of 17.5%.

key_stats.global_market_size: $4.17 billion in 2025 and $5.02 billion in 2026 global smart thermostat market

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from retail thermostat sales, pro-channel HVAC contractor sales, OEM/private-label supply, utility marketplace sales, multifamily and light-commercial deployments, accessories such as remote sensors and power adapters, warranty or installation partnerships, app-enabled services, grid-services partnerships, and energy-management integrations. Hardware margins are pressured by retail discounting and electronics costs, while software, utility demand response, and ecosystem services can improve lifetime economics.
cost_structure: The largest cost buckets are electronic components, displays, sensors, wireless modules, plastics, circuit boards, firmware and app development, cloud connectivity, certification, warranty support, freight, tariffs, retailer fees, contractor-channel support, marketing, and customer service. Gross margins depend heavily on scale, outsourced manufacturing terms, semiconductor availability, product mix between entry-level and premium devices, and the ability to attach sensors, subscriptions, or utility/grid-service revenue.
current_dynamics: The market is still expanding as connected thermostats become a standard energy-efficiency upgrade, but growth is less purely adoption-led than in the 2010s. 2025-2026 competition centers on affordability, Matter interoperability, utility demand response enrollment, compatibility with heat pumps and advanced HVAC systems, and integration into home energy ecosystems. Softer new-home activity in 2026 limits builder-channel demand, while replacement, rebates, utility marketplaces, and HVAC contractor recommendations support ongoing unit sales.
whats_growing: Lower-priced smart thermostats, Wi-Fi and Matter-compatible models, utility bring-your-own-device demand response programs, heat-pump-compatible controls, room sensors, cloud energy reports, pro-installed connected thermostats, and whole-home energy-management platforms are growing. Utility and grid-service use cases are becoming more important because smart thermostats can reduce peak cooling load without requiring large customer behavior changes.
whats_shrinking: Standalone premium differentiation is narrowing as cheaper models add core app control, scheduling, and ecosystem support. Basic non-connected programmable thermostats continue losing share in smart-home and energy-efficiency channels. Growth tied to new construction is under pressure in 2026 because housing starts and residential building activity are weaker than in 2025. Hardware-only margins are also shrinking as retailers and major brands compete around sub-$150 entry models.
recent_developments: 2025-01: ecobee announced Smart Thermostat Essential at CES 2025 at $129.99 in the US, expanding the low-price tier.
2025-01: Resideo introduced the Honeywell Home X2S Smart Thermostat at CES 2025, refreshing its connected thermostat lineup.
2025-06: Parks Associates and Resideo reported that about 20% of smart thermostat homes, roughly 4 million US internet households, were enrolled in demand response programs.
2026-04: Google released a Nest Learning Thermostat software update adding expanded HVAC configuration and Matter bridge support for thermostat sensors.
2026-05: US Census reported May 2026 housing starts at a 1.177 million annual rate, down 8.7% from May 2025, signaling weaker new-install demand.
2026-07: ENERGY STAR data.gov metadata showed the certified smart thermostat dataset last updated July 6, 2026, supporting ongoing model certification and rebate eligibility tracking.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is positive but competitive. Current market forecasts point to high-teens annual growth, helped by energy costs, heat-pump adoption, utility incentives, demand response, and broader smart-home penetration. The strongest manufacturers will pair reliable HVAC compatibility with low-friction installation, interoperability, grid-services capability, and privacy/security assurances. Risks include housing weakness, consumer reluctance around connected-home data, electronics supply-chain exposure, China tariff uncertainty, and retail price compression. A practical 2026 view is that industry revenue growth remains healthy, but profit improvement depends more on scale, channel mix, software services, and utility partnerships than on simple unit sales.
